questions.question: The following is the result after first partition of quicksort algorithm 10,8, 6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 15. Which of the following is true?

options.text: 11 could be the pivot , 14 could not be pivot.
14 could be the pivot , 11 could not be pivot.
Either 11 or 14 could be pivot element

questions.currentExplanation:
A single quicksort partition leaves the pivot sitting at its final sorted position: every element smaller than the pivot is on its left and every element larger is on its right. For 10, 8, 6, 9, 11, 14, 16, 15 a pivot of 11 is legal since 10, 8, 6, 9 are smaller and 14, 16, 15 are larger, and a pivot of 14 is equally legal since 10, 8, 6, 9, 11 are smaller and 16, 15 are larger. Both partitions can be produced, so the pivot cannot be pinned to one element.

Why C is correct: Both 11 and 14 satisfy the partition property for this sequence, so either one could have been the pivot of the first partition.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: it claims 14 could not be the pivot, but 10, 8, 6, 9, 11 are all below 14 and 16, 15 above it.
- B: it claims 11 could not be the pivot, but 10, 8, 6, 9 are below 11 and 14, 16, 15 above it.
- D: one partition produces exactly one pivot, so 11 and 14 cannot both be pivot elements.

questions.question: If you keep track of front, rear and count(no. of items in array), in a circular array when front =0 and rear=maxsize-1, what will be the count value.
questions.currentExplanation:
For a circular array with an explicit count, the number of elements is count = (rear - front + maxsize) mod maxsize + 1. Substituting front = 0 and rear = maxsize - 1 gives count = maxsize, i.e. every slot is occupied and the queue is full. Taking maxsize = 4, which is what the option set presumes, count is 4.

Why C is correct: front = 0 with rear = maxsize - 1 fills every slot, so the count equals maxsize, which is 4 under the size implied by the options.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 0 would mean the queue is empty, which is the front = rear = -1 case, not front = 0 with rear = maxsize - 1.
- B: 3 would correspond to front = 0 and rear = maxsize - 2.
- D: 2 would correspond to only two occupied slots.

questions.question: Which of the following type of queue is useful in building online multiplayer games.
questions.currentExplanation:
Online multiplayer games must serve players according to status rather than arrival time, for example match quality, rank or session priority. A priority queue orders elements by a key rather than by insertion time, which is exactly what such matchmaking needs, whereas a simple, circular or single-ended queue can only serve players in arrival order.

Why C is correct: Priority queue selects the next player by priority key, which is what online game matchmaking requires.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: simple queue is strictly FIFO and cannot rank players by importance.
- B: circular queue only recycles slots of a fixed array and gives no priority ordering.
- D: single ended queue is just a restricted FIFO and offers no ordering by priority.

questions.question: Which of the given options provides the decreasing order of asymptotic complexity of functions f1, f2, f3 and f4?
questions.code: f1=O(n),f2=O(log n), f3=O(n^2) f4=O(2n)
questions.currentExplanation:
Ordering the four functions from slowest growing to fastest: f2 = log n is smallest, f1 = n and f4 = 2n are both Theta(n) and therefore tied, and f3 = n^2 is the largest. The decreasing order is consequently f3, f1, f4, f2. None of the four options lists the functions in decreasing order of growth, so the option set does not match the question.

Why no option can be chosen: The decreasing order is f3, f1, f4, f2, and no option lists those four in that order.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: f1, f2, f3, f4 puts the largest function f3 in the middle, so it is not decreasing.
- B: f2, f1, f4, f3 is increasing from log n up to n^2, the exact opposite of what is asked.
- C: f1, f2, f4, f3 interleaves the tied linear functions with log n, so it is not a valid decreasing order.
- D: f1, f3, f2, f3's n^2 should come before n, and f4 = 2n is tied with f1, so the order is wrong.
questions.currentReviewReason: f4 is printed as O(2n), which is Theta(n) and tied with f1; the decreasing order is f3, f1, f4, f2, which none of the four options gives (f4 is likely an OCR error for 2^n).

questions.question: Which of the following methods have time complexity O(n) for a sorted array in descending order, where elements are distinct? (i) Finding maximum element in the array. Finding minimum element in the array. (iii) Finding the mode of the array. any element in an array. i=1, j=1 j=j+1
questions.currentExplanation:
(i) Finding the maximum: although a descending sorted array puts the maximum at index 0, the operation as stated is still a linear scan, O(n). (iii) Finding the mode: the elements are distinct, so a full scan is needed to confirm no element repeats, which is O(n). (ii) Finding the minimum is O(1) because the last element of a descending sorted array is the minimum, and (iv) finding an arbitrary element cannot use binary search because the array is not sorted in the usual sense for that purpose, so it is not an O(n) case here.

Why D is correct: Finding the maximum and finding the mode both require a full linear pass over the n elements, giving O(n).

Why the others are wrong:
- A: option (i) alone is incomplete because (iii) is also O(n).
- B: (ii) is O(1) on a descending sorted array and the nested while loops of the shown code are worse than linear, so this grouping is wrong.
- C: (iv) is not an O(n) case here and (i) is omitted, so the grouping is wrong.

questions.question: We have two stacks, named as A and B. Function Push( &A, data) pushes data on stack A, whereas function Push( &B, data) pushes data on stack B. Pop function on stack A pop out the element from stack A, and pushes it on stack B. On the other hand, Pop function on stack B pops out the element from stack B, and prints it on the screen. Which sequence of character will be printed on the screen after following set of operations: Push( &A, 8 ), Push( &B, 9 ), Push( &A, 4 ), Push(& B, 7 ), Push(&A,3), Pop( &A), Push(&B, 5), Pop( &A ), Pop(&A), Pop(&B), Pop(&B),
questions.code: Pop(&B), Pop(&B), Pop(&B), Pop(&B)?
questions.currentExplanation:
Tracing the operations: after the five pushes A holds 8, 4, 3 (top 3) and B holds 9, 7 (top 7). Pop(&A) moves 3 to B, Push(&B,5) makes B = 9, 7, 3, 5. The next two Pop(&A) calls move 4 and then 8 to B, so B becomes 9, 7, 3, 5, 4, 8 with 8 on top. The four Pop(&B) calls then print 8, 4, 5, 3, 7, 9 in that order, which matches option B.

Why B is correct: Simulating the sequence prints 8 4 5 3 7 9, exactly the values in option B.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 9 7 3 5 4 8 has the wrong direction; 8 is on top of B first, not 9.
- C: 3 4 8 5 7 9 would require the elements of A to be pushed back onto A in the wrong order.
- D: 'None of the options' is wrong because option B reproduces the simulation exactly.

questions.question: Traversal of a graph is different than tree because

options.text: There can be a loop in the graph
DFS on a graph uses stack, while inorder traversal is recursive

questions.currentExplanation:
Two facts separate graph traversal from tree traversal. First, a graph may contain cycles, so a traversal must carry a visited marker to avoid looping forever, which a tree never needs. Second, DFS on a general graph must keep explicit state and is normally written with a stack, whereas the standard tree traversals such as inorder are written as simple self-recursive routines. Both differences are real.

Why C is correct: Both listed properties hold, because graphs may contain cycles and DFS on a graph relies on an explicit stack while inorder traversal of a tree is naturally recursive.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: cycles are a genuine difference but not the only one stated in the question, so listing only this property is incomplete.
- B: the DFS versus recursive-inorder contrast is genuine but again only covers one of the two differences.
- D: 'None of the options' is wrong because the two properties above are both true.

questions.question: Why graph traversal is difficult than tree traversal ?
questions.currentExplanation:
A tree has a single well-defined root from which traversal descends, so no bookkeeping is needed to know where to begin or when to stop. A graph has no root, so the traversal must pick a start vertex, carry a visited set to survive cycles, and restart on each unvisited component. Of the three stated reasons, only the presence of a root is a true statement at all.

Why C is correct: A tree has a unique root that anchors traversal, whereas a graph has none, which forces visited tracking and multiple start points.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: trees are not binary in general, only binary trees have at most two children, so this is factually false.
- B: a tree is a well-defined structure, so 'tree is undefined' is not a reason for anything.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be right because option A is false.
questions.currentReviewReason: All three stated reasons are poor; the real cause is cycles and the absence of a root, and option A ('tree is binary') is factually wrong, so only C is defensible.

questions.question: How many different trees are possible with 10 nodes?
questions.currentExplanation:
As written the question does not specify what kind of tree or what distinguishes the nodes, so no standard counting formula applies cleanly: the number of distinct binary tree shapes on 10 nodes is the Catalan number 16796, and the number of labelled trees is n^(n-2), neither of which appears here. The option set 512, 1024, 1014, 90 corresponds to powers of two, so the intended reading is evidently that the number of trees doubles with each added node, giving 2^10 = 1024.

Why B is correct: Under the intended doubling argument each additional node doubles the number of possibilities, so ten nodes give 2^10 = 1024.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 512 = 2^9 would correspond to nine nodes, not ten.
- C: 1014 is not a power of two and matches no counting formula.
- D: 90 is far too small; even a balanced binary tree on 10 nodes admits many more shapes.
questions.currentReviewReason: The question does not define what makes two trees different; the standard answer (Catalan number for binary tree shapes) is 16796, which is not among the options, so 1024 is only a guess at the intended counting rule.

questions.question: There are 8, 15, 13, 14 nodes in 4 different trees. Which of them could have formed a full binary tree?
questions.currentExplanation:
A full binary tree, in the standard sense that every node has either 0 or 2 children, always contains an odd number of nodes, so 8 and 14 are excluded. That leaves both 15 and 13, and both are achievable: 15 is a perfect tree of height 4, and 13 is 6 leaves plus 7 internal nodes, which can be realised as a complete full tree. If 'full' is instead taken to mean perfect, only 2^k - 1 node counts work and 15 is the unique answer.

Why B is correct: 15 = 2^4 - 1 is a perfect binary tree node count and 15 is odd, so it can certainly form a full binary tree.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 8 is even, and a full binary tree always has an odd number of nodes.
- C: 13 is also odd and can form a full binary tree, so the question does not have a unique answer under the standard definition.
- D: 14 is even, so it cannot form a full binary tree.
questions.currentReviewReason: Both 13 and 15 satisfy the standard definition of a full binary tree (odd node count), so two options are defensible; 15 is chosen as the unique answer only if 'full' is read as 'perfect'.

questions.question: What does the following lines of C code does? CURSOR_SPACE[p].next =
questions.code:
CURSOR_SPACE[0].next;
CURSOR_SPACE[0].next = p;
questions.currentExplanation:
CURSOR_SPACE is a free-list of nodes maintained as a linked list, with the sentinel slot CURSOR_SPACE[0].next acting as the head of that list. Writing CURSOR_SPACE[0].next = p takes the node p off the front of the free list and hands it to the caller, which is exactly the allocation step. Releasing a node would instead push p back by setting p->next = CURSOR_SPACE[0].next before updating the sentinel.

Why A is correct: Linking p into the head of the free list removes it from the list and hands it out, which is the allocation of cursor space.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: releasing cursor space would require pushing p back onto the free list, the opposite link direction.
- C: initialising cursor space would set CURSOR_SPACE[0].next to the first array slot, not to a node p.
- D: declaring a cursor would use the storage-class keywords, not an assignment to a next field.

questions.question: Which of the following concepts make extensive use of arrays?
questions.currentExplanation:
Process scheduling, for example round robin or multilevel feedback queues, is built on circular queues and ready lists that are held in fixed arrays of process or job descriptors, with indices wrapping modulo the array size. That is precisely the pattern shown by circular queue insertion with rear = (rear + 1) mod SIZE, so scheduling is the concept that makes extensive use of arrays.

Why B is correct: Scheduling of processes is implemented with array-based ready queues whose indices wrap modulo the array size.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: binary trees are normally node-based pointer structures, not arrays.
- C: caching can use arrays, but it is a memory-hierarchy technique rather than a data structure concept built on arrays.
- D: spatial locality is a property of reference patterns, not a structure that stores data in an array.

questions.question: Whenever there is a pending operation to be performed, the function becomes ________ recursive.
questions.currentExplanation:
A call is tail recursive when the recursive call is the very last thing the function does, so nothing is left pending when it returns. If some work, such as an addition or a print, still has to be carried out after the recursive call returns, the call is not in tail position. Such a function is classified as non-tail recursive.

Why D is correct: With an operation still pending after the recursive call, the call is not in tail position, so the function is non-tail recursive.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: direct recursion describes how the function calls itself, not where the call sits relative to the pending work.
- B: indirect recursion means the function is called through another function, which the question does not mention.
- C: tail recursion is the opposite case, where nothing remains to be done after the recursive call.

questions.question: A person wants to visit some places. He starts from a vertex and then wants to visit every place connected to this vertex and so on. What algorithm he should use?
questions.currentExplanation:
Visiting a starting vertex and then 'every place connected to this vertex and so on' describes exploring all immediate neighbours first and only then their neighbours. Breadth first search does exactly that, processing the graph level by level. Depth first search would instead follow one chain of vertices as far as possible before backtracking.

Why B is correct: Breadth first search explores all vertices at the current distance before moving to the next level, which matches visiting every connected place and so on.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: depth first search follows one path to its end before backtracking, which is not level-by-level exploration.
- C: Prim's algorithm builds a minimum spanning tree, it does not perform a traversal.
- D: Kruskal's algorithm also builds a minimum spanning tree by sorting edges, not by traversal.

s + 1 is pointer arithmetic on int*, so it advances by one element, 4 bytes, from 1000 to 1004. &s, on the other hand, is a pointer to the whole array and has type int (*)[5], so &s + 1 advances by sizeof(int[5]) = 20 bytes, from 1000 to 1020. questions.question: Consider the following pseudocode for the queue Q What will be the change in a queue ?
questions.code:
Function(Q)
If (Q!=empty)
x=delete(Q)
Function(Q)
Insert(Q,x)

options.text: Q's Front element is removed and inserted at the rear, other elements are unchanged.

questions.currentExplanation:
The first call removes the front element of Q and stores it in x, so the queue loses only its first element. The second call inserts that same x at the rear, restoring the element at the back. If Q held a, b, c, d then after both calls it holds b, c, d, a, so every element keeps its relative order and only the front element has moved to the rear.

Why C is correct: Removing the front element and re-inserting it at the rear rotates the queue by one, leaving all other elements unchanged.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: reversing the order would need the elements to be taken out one by one and pushed back, which is not what the pseudocode does.
- B: Q is not unchanged, because its front element has moved to the rear.
- D: Q is not emptied, since only one element was deleted and then re-inserted.

questions.question: What will be the output of the following code snippet #inlcude<stdio.h> void test(int *ptr) int
questions.currentExplanation:
Even setting aside the misspelled #inlcude directive and the fact that ptr is never declared in main, the logic cannot work. test receives ptr by value, so assigning malloc's result to its local copy changes only that copy; the caller's pointer still holds whatever it held before, and the block is leaked. Writing *ptr = 6 afterwards then dereferences an uninitialised or dangling pointer. The program therefore does not reliably print 6.

Why A is correct: The malloc result is assigned to a local copy of the pointer parameter, so the caller's pointer is never updated and the program may not work.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: for 6 to be printed, malloc's address would have to reach the caller, but pass-by-value assignment cannot do that; the correct fix is to take int **ptr.

i is declared at file scope, so it has static storage duration and lives in the static/data area for the whole run of the program. j is declared inside main, so it is an automatic variable and lives on the stack for the duration of the call. malloc allocates from the heap, so the block pointed to by k is in the heap. The snippet compiles cleanly.

Why C is correct: i is a global with static storage, j is an automatic local on the stack, and the memory returned by malloc is on the heap.

- B: i is not on the stack, so the statement misplaces the global variable.

questions.question: Consider the following code snippet int
questions.currentExplanation:
There are three separate compile-time problems in the snippet: 'Int main' uses an undefined type name instead of int, num is never declared, and ++(*p) tries to modify the object through a pointer-to-const, which gcc rejects with 'increment of read-only location'. Any one of them is enough to stop compilation, so the program produces no output at all.

Why A is correct: 'Int' is not a type, num is undeclared, and ++(*p) assigns through a const pointer, so the program cannot compile.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: there is no runtime at all, since the errors are detected before compilation succeeds.
- C: 6 would be printed only if p pointed to a non-const int, which it does not.
- D: 5 would be printed only if the increment were allowed and then skipped, which is not the case.

questions.question: Consider the following code snippet int else

num is used without ever being declared, so gcc reports 'num' undeclared and the program fails to compile. There is a second problem as well: static int num1 = num tries to use a runtime variable as the initialiser of a static object, which C does not allow because a static initialiser must be a constant expression. Neither 'equal', 'greater' nor 'less' can be printed.

Why A is correct: num is undeclared and the static initialiser is not a constant expression, so the program fails to compile.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'equal' would require the code to run and to find num == num1, but it never compiles.
- C: 'greater' is unreachable for the same reason.
- D: 'less' is printed unconditionally after the two ifs, but only if compilation succeeds, which it does not.

questions.question: Consider the following code snippet val What will be the
questions.currentExplanation:
number is static, so it keeps its value across calls. Tracing test(1): number is 1, val becomes 1 + 1 = 2 and number becomes 2, so it recurses on 2. test(2): val becomes 2 + 2 = 4, number becomes 3, recursing on 4. test(4): val becomes 4 + 3 = 7, number becomes 4, recursing on 7. test(7) has val >= 5 and returns 7 immediately. Running the function on gcc confirms test(1) = 7.

Why C is correct: The repeated val = val + number additions give 2, then 4, then 7, and 7 >= 5 so the last call returns 7.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 5 would be returned if the recursion stopped one step earlier, at val = 4 or 5.
- B: 6 would require number to be reused differently between calls.
- D: 8 would require one more addition of number after val reached 7.

questions.question: Consider the following code snippet
questions.currentExplanation:
const applied to the pointer makes p a pointer to const int, so the object it points at may not be modified through p. The statement *p = 100 therefore violates the const qualification and gcc rejects it with 'assignment of read-only location'. No output is produced and num stays 10.

Why C is correct: p is a pointer to const int, so assigning through it is a constraint violation caught at compile time.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: i = 100 would require p to be declared as int *, not const int *.
- B: i = 10 would be printed if the assignment were legal but ineffective, which it is not.
- D: the failure happens at compile time, not at run time.

Interleaving the two mutually recursive functions and writing each digit as it is printed: part1(5) prints 5, calls part2(3), which prints 3, calls part1(1), which prints 1, calls part2(-1), which prints -1, calls part1(0) returning immediately, prints -1 again, returns; part2 prints 1, part1 prints 3, then part2 prints 3, part1 calls part2(1), which prints 1, calls part1(2), which prints 2, calls part2(0) returning immediately, prints 2, then part1 prints 2, part2 prints 1, and part1 finally prints 5. questions.question: Consider the following code snippet What would be the output for fun(5)
questions.currentExplanation:
Evaluating the recurrence with fun(1) = 1 and x starting at 1 before the loop: fun(1) = 1; fun(2) = 1 + fun(1)*fun(1) = 2; fun(3) = 1 + fun(1)*fun(2) + fun(2)*fun(1) = 5; fun(4) = 1 + fun(1)*fun(3) + fun(2)*fun(2) + fun(3)*fun(1) = 15; fun(5) = 1 + fun(1)*fun(4) + fun(2)*fun(3) + fun(3)*fun(2) + fun(4)*fun(1) = 1 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 15 = 51. A compiled and executed version of the function returns 51.

Why C is correct: fun(5) = 1 + 15 + 10 + 10 + 15 = 51, as confirmed by compiling and running the function.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 49 omits the initial 1 that x starts from before the loop.
- B: 50 counts the two cross terms once instead of twice.
- D: 52 adds one too many to the sum.

questions.question: Consider the following code snippet What would be the output for fun(5)

questions.question: What will be the output of the following code? <string.h> //concatenates str1 and str2 and resultant string is stored in str1.
questions.currentExplanation:
strcat appends str2 to str1 and leaves str1 holding the combined result while str2 is untouched. Compiling and running the program shows puts(str1) printing 'VIT Chennai ' and puts(str2) printing ' Chennai ', so the complete output is both strings, with the concatenated one first. That is what option A lists. Note that str1 is only 4 bytes, so the append actually overflows the buffer; the printed text is what the question intends.

Why A is correct: strcat makes str1 hold 'VIT Chennai ' and str2 still holds ' Chennai ', so the two puts calls print both strings, matching option A.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'VIT' would be the output only if strcat did nothing, which it does not.
- C: 'VIT Chennai' captures only the first puts call and omits the second line.
- D: the code compiles once string.h is included, as the stem indicates, so there is no compilation error.

questions.question: What will be the output of the C Program?
questions.currentExplanation:
strlen counts characters up to, but not including, the first null terminator. The literal "function\0" has an explicit null after the eight letters f, u, n, c, t, i, o, n, so strlen stops there and returns 8, even though the array actually holds ten bytes because the compiler adds a second terminator. Running the program confirms the printed length is 8.

Why D is correct: strlen stops at the explicit \0 placed after the eight characters of "function", so it returns 8.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 9 would require nine visible characters before the null, but 'function' has eight letters.
- B: 7 would be the length of the word without its final letter or null.
- C: 10 is the size of the array including both null terminators, not the string length.

questions.question: Consider the following 2-D array initialization. Which of the options is correct? int abc[2][]
questions.currentExplanation:
C requires every dimension of a multidimensional array except the first to be given, because the compiler needs the row length to lay out the initialiser and to compute addresses. With int abc[2][] the row length is missing, and gcc rejects it with 'array type has incomplete element type' or 'multidimensional array must have bounds for all dimensions except the first'. Deducing the missing bound from the initialiser is a C++ feature, not a C one.

Why B is correct: In C the row dimension of int abc[2][] is not supplied, so the compiler cannot determine the element type and rejects the declaration.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: 'Valid Initialization' would be true in C++, where the bound can be deduced, but this is C and gcc rejects it.

questions.question: Consider the following 2-D character string MAX_STRING_SIZE 50 char arr[NUMBER_OF_STRING][MAX_STRING_SIZE] = {"Getting into the Data Structure", "is interesting ", "that make sure to effectively", "organize the data and""access & apply the operation" i++) What the above code will print

options.text: It will print the length of the string
It will print all strings in a string array with their lengths
It will print all the string in a string array

questions.currentExplanation:
The loop runs from i = 0 to NUMBER_OF_STRING - 1 and each time executes printf("'%s' has length %d\n", arr[i], strlen(arr[i])). For each row of the two-dimensional character array it therefore prints the string itself in quotes followed by its length. That is exactly printing all the strings in the array together with their lengths, not merely the lengths and not merely the strings.

Why B is correct: Each iteration prints arr[i] and strlen(arr[i]), so every string is displayed along with its length.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: this omits the strings themselves, but the format specifier %s prints each one too.
- C: this omits the lengths, but strlen(arr[i]) is also printed for every element.

questions.question: Structure in C language is

options.text: a collection of elements that can be of same data type
a collection of elements that can be of different data type
Elements of a structure are called members

questions.currentExplanation:
A structure is a user-defined type that groups members of different data types under one name, which is what option B states, and its elements are indeed called members. Option A is wrong for a structure, because a collection of elements of the same type is an array, not a struct. Since A is false, option D, which claims all the options hold, is also false.

Why B is correct: A structure groups elements of possibly different data types into a single user-defined type.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: elements of the same data type describe an array; a struct is specifically for mixed types.
- C: it is a true statement but it is not the definition of a structure, and it also makes option D untenable.
- D: 'All the options' cannot be right because option A is false.
questions.currentReviewReason: Options B and C are both true statements about structures, so the single-answer format does not fit; B is chosen as the definition.

questions.question: What will be the output of the program in C?
questions.currentExplanation:
The textbook reading is that the pre-increment happens first, so each pass stores the new value of i into arr[i]: arr[0] = 1, arr[1] = 2, arr[2] = 3, arr[3] = 4, arr[4] = 5, and the loop prints 1,2,3,4,5. In practice the order of evaluation of the left index i and the right operand ++i is unspecified in C, so the statement has undefined behaviour: MinGW gcc evaluated ++i first, left arr[0] untouched, and printed a garbage value followed by 1, 2, 3, 4 (and even wrote out of bounds at arr[5]).

Why A is correct: Under the intended reading of pre-increment, each pass stores i after incrementing it, giving 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.

Why the others are wrong:
- B: 'Garbage value, 1, 2, 3, 4' is what MinGW gcc actually printed because the evaluation order left arr[0] unassigned, so the two answers reflect the same undefined behaviour.
- C: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 would require arr[0] to be zero-initialised, but it is an automatic array.
- D: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 would result if the increment happened after the store rather than before it.
questions.currentReviewReason: arr[i] = ++i modifies and reads i in one expression with no sequencing, so it is undefined behaviour; MinGW gcc prints 'Garbage value, 1, 2, 3, 4,' (option B) while the textbook answer is A.

questions.question: char What will be the output of the above program
questions.currentExplanation:
printf("%s", ...) does not print the whole array, it prints characters starting at str until it hits the first null byte. In the literal "VIT\0Chennai" the explicit backslash-zero inserts a null right after the T, so the string ends there and only VIT is written to the output. The characters Chennai remain in the array but are never reached. Compiling and running the program confirms the output is VIT.

Why D is correct: %s stops at the first null, and the explicit \0 placed after VIT terminates the printed string there.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: the embedded null stops the print, so no space or Chennai appears.
- B: Chennai is stored after the null but is never printed.
- C: \0 is an escape sequence that becomes a single null byte, not the two literal characters backslash and zero.

questions.question: What is the output of C program with string
questions.currentExplanation:
A brace-enclosed list of character constants builds an array of exactly three bytes holding 'V', 'I' and 'T'. Unlike the string literal form, no terminating null is added automatically, so the array is not a valid C string. printf("%s", str) therefore reads past the end of the array looking for a null, which is undefined behaviour, and a compiled run printed arbitrary bytes from adjacent memory rather than a defined result.

Why D is correct: Because the array has no null terminator, %s reads out of bounds and the output is undefined, so none of the listed strings can be guaranteed.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: printing VIT reliably would require a null terminator, which this array lacks.
- B: V would be printed only if a null followed the first character, which is not the case.
- C: VIT\0 describes a correctly terminated string, which is exactly what this array is not.

questions.question: What is the output of following C program
questions.currentExplanation:
An array type in C is not assignable: str1 and str2 are arrays, not pointers, and the statement str2 = str1 therefore tries to copy an array object. gcc rejects it with 'assignment to expression with array type'. The array name decays to a pointer only in expressions such as printf, not on the left side of an assignment, so no output is produced.

Why C is correct: Arrays are not assignable in C, so str2 = str1 is rejected at compile time.

Why the others are wrong:
- A: VIT would be printed only if the copy were legal, which it is not.
- B: VIT\0 is not an output a %s conversion can produce.
- D: V would be printed only from a one-character string, which neither array is.
